parole.significato: Used to form the diminutives of nouns in Hiberno-English.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish -ín (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: darling
parole.testo: From Irish a chuisle (“O pulse (of my heart)”).

parole.significato: Expanded polystyrene foam, such as is used in insulation.
parole.testo: From aero- (or the Irish aer) + board, or from a company of a similar name which manufactures polystyrene insulation products in Ireland.

parole.significato: Dear, darling (as a term of endearment).
parole.testo: From Irish a (vocative particle) + lenited form of grá (“love”).

parole.significato: A kind of Irish poem, developed during the late 17th and 18th centuries, in which Ireland appears to the poet in a visi…
parole.testo: From Irish aisling.

parole.significato: child
parole.testo: From Irish a leanbh (“O child”).

parole.significato: An ancient Irish public national assembly called upon the death of a king, queen, notable sage or warrior as part of an…
parole.testo: From Irish aonach, from Old Irish óenach, from óen (“one”).

parole.significato: A medium weight of yarn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish Árainn.

parole.significato: A high king of Ireland.
parole.testo: From Irish ardrí.

parole.significato: A form of address to a male friend or young man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish a mhic (“literally, my son”), from a (“vocative marker”) + mhic (“lenited form of mic”), variant of mac (“son”).

parole.significato: darling, sweetheart
parole.testo: From Irish a mhuirnín (“my darling”, literally “O darling (vocative)”), from Middle Irish múirn, from Proto-Celtic *mori, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to care for”), see also Latin memoria, Ancient Greek μέριμνα (mérimna, “care”).

parole.significato: Undyed white homespun woolen yarn or cloth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish báinín, from bán (“white”) + -ín (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A division of land in Ireland equal to 480 Irish acres (approximately 315 hectares or 778 statute acres) of arable land.
parole.testo: From Irish baile biataigh (“victualler's townland”), from baile (“home”) + betagh (“victualer”).

parole.significato: An Irish measure of two feet (61 cm) in length.
parole.testo: From Irish banlámh (“cubit”), from Middle Irish bannlám, from bann (“a measure”) + lám (“hand, arm”).

parole.significato: A female spirit, usually taking the form of a woman whose mournful wailing warns of an impending death.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish bean sí, from Old Irish ben síde (literally “woman of the fairy mound”). The term banshee entered English in 1771.

parole.significato: An Irish yeasted bread with sultanas and raisins.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish bairín breac.

parole.significato: A cattle-fort; a building used to shelter cattle.
parole.testo: From Irish bán, alternative form of bábhún (“walled enclosure”).

parole.significato: Woven wool or flannel; especially undyed, unbleached wool.
parole.testo: From Irish báinín (“(undyed) wool”), from bán (“white”) + -ín (“-een”).

parole.significato: A mountain pass.
parole.testo: From Irish bealach.

parole.significato: Synonym of Belleek ware.
parole.testo: From Irish Béal Leice.

parole.significato: A tenant that provides food for a household. On Anglo-Norman manors, these workers were servile to their lords.
parole.testo: From Irish biatach, from Middle Irish bíatach (“providing food”), ultimately from bíad (“food”).

parole.significato: A type of banshee whose cry indicates someone's impending death.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish badhb, a variant of badhbh.

parole.significato: A fellow, a man; especially an ordinary man, a man on the street.
parole.testo: Origin unknown; the following borrowings have been hypothesized: * From a modern Celtic language, such as Irish bloc (“block”) or Scottish Gaelic ploc (“large, stubborn person”, literally “block of wood”), themselves borrowings from English block * From Hindustani لوک (lok) / लोक (lok, “people, folk

parole.significato: to hinder, stop
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish bac (“to hinder”).

parole.significato: unsteady, wobbly, tottering, rickety (likely to fall over)
parole.testo: From Irish bacaidí, from bacach (“lame”).

parole.significato: crooked
parole.testo: Derived from Irish bac (“bend”).

parole.significato: A type of frame drum used in Irish music struck traditionally with an animal bone, or in modern times, with a piece of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish bodhrán.

parole.significato: An area of decayed vegetation (particularly sphagnum moss) which forms a wet spongy ground too soft for walking.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bog (originally chiefly in Ireland and Scotland), from Irish and Scottish Gaelic bogach (“soft, boggy ground”), from Old Irish bog (“soft”), from Proto-Celtic *buggos (“soft, tender”) + Old Irish -ach, from Proto-Celtic *-ākos. The frequent use to form compounds regardi

parole.significato: A piglet.
parole.testo: From Irish banbhán (“piglet”), altered under the influence of the surname Bonham.

parole.significato: Sour, soured, fermented or curdled milk; acidophilus milk.
parole.testo: Said to be from Irish bainne (“milk”) + clábair (“muddied”) (see English clabber) or Scots Gaelic cognates thereof, with the anglicization of the first element influenced by bonny.

parole.significato: A company of Irish herdsmen, or a single herdsman, wandering from place to place with flocks and herds, and living on t…
parole.testo: From Irish buaile (“cattle enclosure, summer pasturage for cows”), from Old Irish bó (“cow”) or būale, probably from Latin bovile (“cattle stall”) or bubile, from Latin bos (“cow, bull, ox”) (bov-).

parole.significato: A narrow, frequently unpaved, rural road in Ireland, often characterised by a ridge of grass growing in the middle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish bóithrín, from bóthar (“road”) and -ín (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A foolish person.
parole.testo: From Irish bastún.

parole.significato: A traditional Irish potato pancake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish bacstaí.

parole.significato: A judge or lawgiver in ancient Celtic Ireland.
parole.testo: From an Anglicized oblique form (such as genitive singular breitheamhan or dative singular breitheamhain) of Irish breitheamh, from Old Irish brithem, from breth (“judgment”).

parole.significato: An Irish housemaid.
parole.testo: English form of the Irish saints' name Brighid, Brigid. Doublet of Bride.

parole.significato: A strong dialectal accent, usually Irish or Scottish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish bróg (“boot, shoe”), from Old Irish bróc (“shoe, greave, legging, hose, breeches”), likely from Old Norse brók (“breeches”), from Proto-Germanic *brōks (“breeches”). The "accent" sense may instead be derived from Irish barróg (“a hold (on the tongue)”).

parole.significato: a poor young man of the lower Anglo-Irish gentry who aspires to the habits and dress of the wealthy.
parole.testo: From Irish boicín, the diminutive of boc. Equivalent to buck + -een.

parole.significato: A natural depression in a stone, often filled with water and sometimes pebbles.
parole.testo: From Irish bullán.

parole.significato: Any of various ancient and traditional Irish football games.
parole.testo: From Irish caid (“stuffed ball; football”).

parole.significato: A travelling tinker or a tramp.
parole.testo: From Irish ceard (“a tinker”).

parole.significato: Of land: low-lying and near a river, and thus regularly submerged.
parole.testo: From Irish caladh (“meadow by a riverbank”), from Old Irish calad (“shore, landing, port”), probably a noun use of calad (“hard”, adjective), from Proto-Celtic *kaletos (“cruel; hard; strong”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlH-eto- (“cold”) (in the sense of something frozen and thus hard), fro

parole.significato: Synonym of shinty (“stick used to hit the ball in the game of shinty”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish camán.

parole.significato: A women's stick-and-ball sport from Ireland, almost identical to hurling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish camógaíocht.

parole.significato: Irish moss (Chondrus crispus)
parole.testo: From Irish carraigín (“Irish moss”), from carraig (“rock”).

parole.significato: A gambler in Ireland.
parole.testo: From Irish cearrbhach; compare Scottish Gaelic cearrach, from ceàrrbhag (“the left hand”), from ceàrr (“left”).

parole.significato: In early Ireland, a ringfort or a circular stone structure used for defense.
parole.testo: From Irish caiseal, from Old Irish caisel, from Latin castellum. Doublet of castell, castellum, castle, and château.

parole.significato: A sailing boat with a single sail, usually rigged on a gaff spar, used for fishing in New England and later adapted for…
parole.testo: According to Watkins, the first element is related to the animal cat and has correlations in Dutch kat (“vessel with wide fore and aft”), Medieval Latin gatus, gattus, Old French chat, a war machine or portable shed for protecting sapping operations, or a boat with such a shed, and Middle French cha

parole.significato: An ancient Irish fortification of stone or earthwork.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cathair.

parole.significato: An Irish beret, formerly worn by peasants, later also adopted for army use.
parole.testo: From Irish cáibín, from cába (“cape”), from cappa (“cape”)

parole.significato: The speaker of Dáil Éireann
parole.testo: From Irish ceann (“head”) + comhairle (“[of] council”).

parole.significato: A social event with traditional Irish or Scottish music and dancing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish céilí (“Irish dancing session”), Scottish Gaelic ceilidh.

parole.significato: An Irish Republican, especially one who has supported the armed struggle.
parole.testo: From Irish tiocfaidh, from the Republican slogan tiocfaidh ár lá (“our day will come”), perhaps punning on etymologies 1 and/or 2.

parole.significato: A left-handed person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish ciotóg, from Proto-Celtic *(s)kīttos.

parole.significato: Sour or curdled milk.
parole.testo: Shortening of bonny clabber, from Irish bainne clábar (“mud, thick milk for churning”) or a Scots Gaelic cognate thereof; the latter is probably related to láib (“dirt, mud, filth”).

parole.significato: A large wickerwork basket for carrying produce or turf.
parole.testo: From Irish cliabh (“basket”).

parole.significato: An old dry-stone hut with a corbelled roof, commonly found on the southwest Irish coast.
parole.testo: From Irish clochán.

parole.significato: A mischievous, potentially malicious fairy, akin to the leprechaun, that greatly loves drinking and tends to haunt brew…
parole.testo: From Irish clutharachán, from Irish cluthar (“sheltered, cosy; secretive”) + Irish -achán (“diminutive suffix”) (compare same suffix in Irish leipreachán and lucharachán (“leprechaun”)). William Butler Yeats, citing folklorist Nicholas O'Kearney, derives it from clobhair-ceann, from clobhair (“hunch

parole.significato: The successor to the founder of a religious institution.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish comharba.

parole.significato: A traditional Irish dish made from mashed potatoes and cabbage or kale, with scallions, butter, salt and pepper added.
parole.testo: From Irish cál ceannann (literally “white-faced cabbage”).

parole.significato: A girl.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cailín.

parole.significato: Any of various alcoholic drinks made with lemon juice, sugar, and carbonated water.
parole.testo: * As an English surname, variant of Colin. * As an Irish and Manx surname, from Ó Coileáin (“descendant of Coileán”), see Cullen, McQuillan, and McCallion. * As a French surname, Americanized from Collin and Colette. * As a Slovene surname, Americanized from Kolenc, from koleno (“knee”) and the obso

parole.significato: A pony of a particular breed native to this Irish district.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish Conamara, from Conmhaicne Mara (literally “the Conmhaicne of the sea”), a branch of an ancient native tribe named Conmhaicne (literally “descendants of Conmhac”).

parole.significato: Cool; all right; fine.
parole.testo: Reduplication of cool, influenced by Irish English ruaille buaille (“commotion”), from Irish ruaille buaille.

parole.significato: A lichen that produces a purple dye.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish. Doublet of purple.

parole.significato: A riverine marsh in Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish corcach (“bog, marsh, swamp”).

parole.significato: To levy certain exactions or tribute upon; to lodge and eat at the expense of.
parole.testo: From Irish cuid oíche (“night's supper”) or cóisir (“banquet; festive party”).

parole.significato: A small, crudely-formed boat.
parole.testo: From Irish coite, coit (“small boat”), possibly from Medieval Latin cattia (“pan”).

parole.significato: Something or someone that spoils an otherwise enjoyable event.
parole.testo: From craic (borrowed from Irish craic, itself borrowed from Northern English crack, inherited from Middle English crak (“loud conversation, bragging talk”)) + killer.

parole.significato: An artificial island, used in prehistoric and medieval times in Scotland and Ireland for dwelling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish crannóg, from Middle Irish crannóc.

parole.significato: creature
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish créatúr.

parole.significato: An edible red alga; dulse.
parole.testo: From Irish creathnach.

parole.significato: A hill or mountain in Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cruach. Doublet of rick.

parole.significato: An Irish food made from pigs' feet, usually boiled.
parole.testo: From Irish crúibín.

parole.significato: To beg for mercy; to give up, admit defeat, surrender; indicate submission, such as when wrestling.
parole.testo: Unknown. Uncle may be an anglicization of Irish anacal (“protection”).

parole.significato: An unsophisticated rural person; a rustic or provincial.
parole.testo: Possibly from Kiltimagh, a town in County Mayo, Ireland, or from Irish coillte (“woods”). Possibly a corruption of the shortening of agricultural to culch + -ie.

parole.significato: An Irish unit of account equivalent to the theoretical value of a bondmaid.
parole.testo: From Irish cumhal.

parole.significato: An Irish boat, constructed like a coracle, and originally the same shape; now a boat of similar construction but conven…
parole.testo: From Irish curach, corrach, from Proto-Celtic *korukos (“boat”).

parole.significato: A middle-aged white man exhibiting a sense of entitlement or white privilege.
parole.testo: Unknown. A twentieth-century invention, possibly from a rare Irish surname of obscure meaning, possibly from Dara or Daragh, meaning "oak". parole.significato: Someone from Barnsley
parole.testo: From Irish An Daingean, Daingean Uí Chúi (“fort of Ó Cúis”), from daingean (“fortress”).

parole.significato: A drink taken on departure.
parole.testo: From Irish deoch an dorais and Scottish Gaelic deoch an dorais (“literally, 'door drink'”), from deoch (“a drink”) and dorais (“door”).

parole.significato: sulk, huff
parole.testo: From Irish dod (“sullenness, anger”).

parole.significato: A type of coarse tweed made in this county.
parole.testo: Anglicization of Irish Dún na nGall (literally “fort of the foreigners or strangers”).

parole.significato: A brawl or fracas; a scene of chaos.
parole.testo: Named from Donnybrook Fair, a notoriously disorderly event, held annually from 1204 until the middle of the 19th century. The town of Donnybrook comes from the Irish Domhnach Broc (“The Church of Saint Broc”).

parole.significato: A potato.
parole.testo: From Irish Ó Donndubháin (“descendant of (a person named) brown & black”), from donn (“brown”) and dubh (“black”).

parole.significato: A type of ancient Irish war-horn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish dord (“buzz, drone; dord”).

parole.significato: An idiot.
parole.testo: From Irish Ó Dubhghaill (“descendant of Dougal”).

parole.significato: A type of Irish sausage made from pigs' blood, suet, and salt; an Irish version of black pudding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish drisín.

parole.significato: A small hill or ridge of hills.
parole.testo: From Irish druim, Scottish Gaelic druim (“back, ridge”).

parole.significato: An elongated hill or ridge of glacial drift.
parole.testo: From Irish droim (“back, ridge”) + English diminutive suffix -lin (“variant of -ling”).

parole.significato: A division of a poem, especially an epic poem or a Scottish poem; a canto.
parole.testo: From Irish and Scottish Gaelic duan, from Middle Irish dúan, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂p-no- (compare Old Armenian տաւն (tawn, “feast, celebration”), Ancient Greek δαπάνη (dapánē, “cost”), Old Norse tafn (“sacrificial animal”) and Latin damnum (“damage”)), from *deh₂p- (“to sacrifice”).

parole.significato: A short-stemmed Irish pipe made out of clay.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish dúidín.

parole.significato: A noose of string, metal wire, or hair used to snare an animal, especially a fish.
parole.testo: Probably from Irish dul, dol (“loop, noose, snare”).

parole.significato: A black-clad (usually male) horserider in Irish folklore which carries its severed head like a lantern and may be repel…
parole.testo: From Irish dulachán, from dubh (“black”) + another word (compare lucharachán (“elf, dwarf”)), possibly originally a term for a dark or sullen person (compare the surname Dullahan) and only subsequently applied to the spirit.

parole.significato: A seaweed of a reddish-brown color (Palmaria palmata) which is sometimes eaten, as in Scotland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish duileasc, Scottish Gaelic duileasg; compare Welsh delysg.

parole.significato: An ancient or medieval fortification; especially a hill-fort in Scotland or Ireland.
parole.testo: From Irish dún or Scottish Gaelic dùn, from Proto-Celtic *dūnom (“fortress”). Cognate with Welsh dinas (“city”). Doublet of town.

parole.significato: A fine paid as compensation for violent crimes.
parole.testo: From Irish éiric.

parole.significato: Ireland forever.
parole.testo: From Irish Éire go brách or Éirinn go brách.

parole.significato: A long, narrow, sinuous ridge created by deposits from a stream running beneath a glacier.
parole.testo: From Irish eiscir (“esker, glacial ridge”).

parole.significato: The acute accent as used in Irish orthography to mark a long vowel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish fada (“long”).

parole.significato: A pin badge worn to indicate a fluency in, or a willingness to speak, the Irish language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish fáinne (“ring”). Doublet of fawny.

parole.significato: A finger ring.
parole.testo: From Irish fáinne (“ring”). Doublet of fainne.

parole.significato: A phantom of hunger, resembling an emaciated man.
parole.testo: From Irish [Term?] (literally “man of hunger/famine”).

parole.significato: An Irish festival, usually including folk music, dancing, and sports.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish feis.

parole.significato: Generous (often in an ironic sense).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish flaithiúlach.

parole.significato: An Irish music festival with competitions for the best performance on various instruments.
parole.testo: From Irish fleadh, classical/dialectal/superseded spelling of fleá, from Old Irish fled, from Proto-Celtic *wlidā.

parole.significato: The creation of sound effects, and their addition to film and TV images.
parole.testo: From the surname Foley, itself from Irish Ó Foghlú and Old Irish Ó Foghladha (“plunderer”). The meanings related to sound effects are named after sound effects pioneer Jack Foley.

parole.significato: To bustle about in a purposeless way; fidget.
parole.testo: Borrowing of Irish fústar.

parole.significato: The bilberry or whortleberry (Vaccinium myrtillus).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish fraochán (“blueberry, bilberry”).

parole.significato: Someone who speaks Irish fluently or often.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Irish Gaeilgeoir

parole.significato: A member of an ethnic group in Ireland, Scotland and the Isle of Man, whose language is one that is Gaelic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish Gael, alt. Gaol, from earlier Gaoidheal, cognate with Scottish Gaelic Gàidheal and Manx Gael, from Middle Irish Gaídel, from Old Irish Goídel (“Irishman”), a loanword from Old Welsh Guoidel (“wild man, warrior”) (also recorded as a personal name in the Book of Llandaff), from Pro

parole.significato: A school in which Irish is the working language.
parole.testo: From Irish, from Gael (“Gael, Gaelic person”) + scoil (“school”).

parole.significato: An officially recognised area where the Irish language is the predominant language in daily use.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish Gaeltacht.

parole.significato: A mercenary warrior élite among Gaelic-Norse clans residing in the Western Isles of Scotland and Scottish Highlands fro…
parole.testo: From Irish gallóglach (“foreign soldier”), from Gall (“foreigner, non-Gaelic person”) + óglách (“soldier”).

parole.significato: In abundance.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm Borrowed from Irish go leor and Scottish Gaelic gu leòr, gu leòir (“till sufficient, enough, plenty”) (compare Manx dy liooar), from Irish go, Scottish Gaelic gu (“to; till, until”) + Irish leor, Scottish Gaelic leòr (“ample, sufficient”); go, gu are derived from Old Irish co, cu (“wi

parole.significato: A member of the Gardaí: an Irish national police officer
parole.testo: From Irish Garda (“guardian”), from Irish Garda Síochána (“Guardian of the Peace”) and Garda Síochána na hÉireann (“Guardian of the Peace of Ireland”) after the model of the French Third Republic's civilian French gardiens de la paix, from Old French guarde, from guarder (“to guard”), from Frankish

parole.significato: A young farm boy.
parole.testo: From Irish garsún, from Old French garçun. Doublet of garçon.

parole.significato: A (generally magical) vow, obligation or injunction placed upon someone to do or not do something, which typically brin…
parole.testo: Borrowed, like English geis, from Irish geis (“injunction; taboo, prohibition, spell”). The pronunciation resembles Irish geis, though the spelling matches its synonymous but heterophonous alternative form geas.

parole.significato: Synonym of geas or geis, mistakenly treated as a singular.
parole.testo: Irish geasa, the plural of both geis and geas.

parole.significato: Synonym of geas (“a mystical injunction: a prohibition, or obligation/compulsion”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish geis.

parole.significato: A lunatic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish geilt.

parole.significato: Salmo stomachicus, a trout found in Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish giolla rua (literally “red fellow”), because of its distinctive colouring. See also McElroy.

parole.significato: A young girl.
parole.testo: From Irish girseach.

parole.significato: A secluded and narrow valley, especially one with a river running through it; a depression between hills; a dale.
parole.testo: From Middle English glen, borrowed from Irish gleann and Scottish Gaelic gleann, Old and Middle Irish glend, glenn (“mountain valley”), from Proto-Celtic *glendos (“valley”), hypothetically from Proto-Indo-European *glend- (“shore”) but the word may have been borrowed from a non-Indo-European substr

parole.significato: A mass of matted hair worn down over the eyes, formerly common in Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish glib.

parole.significato: A twelfth part of a ploughland / carucate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish gníomh, from Old Irish gním, from Proto-Celtic *gnīmus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.

parole.significato: The mouth.
parole.testo: Probably from Irish gob, Scottish Gaelic gob (“beak, mouth”).

parole.significato: A glob of saliva and/or phlegm projected out of a person's mouth.
parole.testo: From Irish gob (“mouth”) + seile (“spittle”).

parole.significato: A foolish person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish gám (“booby, dolt”).

parole.significato: Usury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish gaimbín (“monetary interest”).

parole.significato: An egg.
parole.testo: From Irish and Scottish Gaelic gog / gug, cf. googie, from gugaí / gogaí (“sound made by chickens, baby name for chicken, baby name for egg" (i.e. gug-gug-gugaí)”).

parole.significato: An egg.
parole.testo: From Irish and Scottish Gaelic gugaí/gogaí/gogaidh, a nursery word for an egg.

parole.significato: A young boy, a servant boy; a lackey.
parole.testo: From Irish garsún, from Old French garçun. Doublet of garçon.

parole.significato: To irritate or annoy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish griog.

parole.significato: Love, affection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish grá.

parole.significato: A serving of the beverage.
parole.testo: An Anglicization of Irish Mac Aonghusa (literally “son of Angus”).

parole.significato: An urchin or delinquent.
parole.testo: Perhaps from gutter, or guttersnipe. Or possibly from Irish gaotaire (“a windbag, someone who talks too much”).

parole.significato: Large amount; load.
parole.testo: From Irish gabháil.

parole.significato: A hairy caterpillar.
parole.testo: Possibly from hairy + Irish malaí (literally “eyebrows”)

parole.significato: A lazy person.
parole.testo: From Irish aindeiseoir (“a sickly person, a wretch”).

parole.significato: To act as a hooligan (etymology 1, noun sense 1).
parole.testo: Probably a variant of the Irish surname Houlihan, 1890s.

parole.significato: A confused sound of a crowd of people shouting or speaking simultaneously; an uproar.
parole.testo: In early use, the noun is often mentioned as a cry by Irish people, and so is possibly borrowed from Irish; compare Irish ababú, abú (“used as a battle cry”), and Scottish Gaelic ub, ub, ubub (“used to express contempt, etc.”), ubh ubh (“used to express disgust”). The verb is derived from the noun.

parole.significato: Secret, clandestine, sly.
parole.testo: Unknown; perhaps from Anglo-Irish cuggermugger (“a whispering, a low-voiced gossiping”), from Irish cogar (“whisper”). Compare also Scots hudge-mudge, hody-moke, Swedish mjugg (“stealth, secrecy”).

parole.significato: The fruit of the dog rose; a rosehip.
parole.testo: From Johnny + alteration of Irish mogóir (“haw, rosehip”).

parole.significato: poultry, etc., required by the lease to be paid in kind by a tenant to the landlord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cáin.

parole.significato: A prolonged wail for a deceased person.
parole.testo: From Irish caoin (“to lament, keen”).

parole.significato: Sharp, shrill, especially of a sound.
parole.testo: From keen + -ing, from Irish caoin.

parole.significato: A beetle.
parole.testo: From Irish ciaróg.

parole.significato: Kelly green.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish Ó Ceallaigh. Doublet of Kellogg and Callahan.

parole.significato: A basket of branches and stones placed underwater as the base of a causeway.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cis (“basket”). Doublet of cesta, chest, cist, and kist

parole.significato: Any cloth worn over the head or shoulders as a shawl, blindfold, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cuideog.

parole.significato: A piece of small firewood or kindling; dibber
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cipín (“stick used for planting; matchstick”).

parole.significato: A basket used in Ireland, mainly for carrying turf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish cis, ceis (“basket, hamper”). Doublet of cesta.

parole.significato: to mutter or complain sullenly
parole.testo: From Irish cnáimhseáil (“grumbling, complaining”).

parole.significato: Water; any weak alcoholic beverage.
parole.testo: Probably from Irish lag (“weak”), from Old Irish lac, from Proto-Celtic *laggos, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₁g-.

parole.significato: A pile of stones, similar to a cairn, marking a grave.
parole.testo: From Irish leacht (“grave, gravemound”).

parole.significato: A guillemot.
parole.testo: From Irish lamhaidh, from Old Norse tangvé, langvé. Cognate with Icelandic langvía, lómvia, Faroese lomvigi, Norwegian langve, lomvi. Compare also French lare (“seagull”).

parole.significato: A type of diminutive, solitary fairy or sprite, traditionally depicted as a small, bearded man wearing a green coat and…
parole.testo: From Irish leipreachán, luprachán, from Middle Irish luchrupán, from Old Irish luchorpán. See also Irish lucharachán. The word's further etymology is disputed; it is traditionally explained as a compound containing lú (“small”, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-) + corp (“body”, which is from Latin

parole.significato: A humorous, often bawdy verse of five anapaestic lines, with the rhyme scheme aabba, and typically having an 8–8–5–5–8…
parole.testo: From the Irish town name Limerick, Irish Luimneach [ˈl̪ˠɪmʲənʲəx].

parole.significato: A big, lazy man; a loafer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish liúdramán (“loafer”).

parole.significato: A lake or long, narrow inlet, especially in Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish loch (from Old Irish loch), from Proto-Celtic *loku (“lake, pool”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“pond, pool”). Doublet of lay, loch, and Looe.

parole.significato: A type of one-eared spade used in Ireland.
parole.testo: From Irish láí (“spade”), from Middle Irish láige (“spade”).

parole.significato: Term of endearment.
parole.testo: From Irish mo chroí (literally “my heart”).

parole.significato: My darling, my dear.
parole.testo: From Irish mo chuisle (“my pulse”).

parole.significato: To ruin or destroy.
parole.testo: Calque of Irish caca dhéanamh de rud.

parole.significato: Nonsense; rubbish.
parole.testo: Of unknown origin; the word was popularized by the Irish-American cartoonist Thomas Aloysius (“Tad”) Dorgan (1877–1929), who started using it in cartoons on March 9, 1922. Maybe from Irish mallachtóireacht or Greek μαλακίες (malakíes)

parole.significato: Plasticine; modelling clay.
parole.testo: From Irish marla, from Middle English marle. Doublet of marl.

parole.significato: darling, sweetheart
parole.testo: Hiberno-English, from Irish mo mhuirnín (“my darling”) (diminutive of muirn (“affection”)).

parole.significato: An expression of sorrow; alas.
parole.testo: Anglo-Irish, from Irish mo bhrón, from mo (“my”) + brón (“grief”).

parole.significato: myself.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish mé féin (“myself”).

parole.significato: bad luck
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish mí-ádh.

parole.significato: A merman or mermaid in Scottish and Irish Gaelic folklore.
parole.testo: Hiberno-English, from Irish murúch (“mermaid”).

parole.significato: A communal drinking vessel used in Gaelic times for drinking mead. It had squared sides and one drank from a corner. Al…
parole.testo: From Irish meadar, from Old Irish metar, from Latin metrum. Doublet of metre, meter, and metron.

parole.significato: A person who is poor but eternally optimistic, believing that "something will turn up", like the fictional character Wi…
parole.testo: A name likely coined by Charles Dickens, evidently reminiscent of common Irish, Scots, and Scottish Gaelic surnames starting with Mc-, Mac-, both from Old Irish macc (“son, child”) (see more there). For the second particle, compare names like Aubrey; similar surnames like M(a)cAubrey are attested ar

parole.significato: A disagreeable or incompetent person.
parole.testo: From the 1930s, origin unknown. Suggestions include a variant of British slang moke (“donkey”); a variant of US slang mooch (“a sponger, beggar, idler”); Irish muc (“pig”); Dutch mok, German Mocke, Mucke (both dialectal for “sow” and hence “slovenly or bothersome woman/person”); a corruption of Ital

parole.significato: A girlfriend.
parole.testo: Alternative form of mot (“woman; wife”), likely under influence from Irish maith (“goodness”).

parole.significato: A floral whitework embroidery originating in the town of Mountmellick in County Laois, Ireland, in the early 19th centu…
parole.testo: From Irish.

parole.significato: A person who lives in a Gaeltacht area of Ireland.
parole.testo: An anglicisation of Irish muintir na hAite (literally “people of the place”).

parole.significato: To swindle by means of the Murphy game confidence trick.
parole.testo: From Irish Ó Murchadha (“descendant of Murrough”), Mac Murchaidh (“Son of Murrough”), etc. See Muircath.

parole.significato: An expression of surprise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish muise; perhaps originally a minced oath for Muire (“Mary”).

parole.significato: Someone who acts from self-interest, rather than the common good or the national interest.
parole.testo: From Irish mé féin (“myself”) + -er.

parole.significato: Don't worry about it; never mind.
parole.testo: From Irish ná bac leis (don't bother with it).

parole.significato: A grey gurnard (Trigla gurnardus, now Eutrigla gurnadus), a fish of European waters.
parole.testo: Derived from Irish cnúdán.

parole.significato: descendant of; used to form Irish patronymic surnames.
parole.testo: From Irish Ó. Unrelated to English o' (“of”).

parole.significato: A single character in this alphabet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish ogham, from Middle Irish ogam, from Proto-Celtic *ogmos (“furrow, path”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂óǵmos. The Irish word is frequently folk-etymologized as og-úaim, referring to ogham being supposedly made by the point of a sharp weapon, but this approach faces serious phonolo

parole.significato: In Irish history, a man of science or learning, equivalent to a university professor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish ollamh, from Old Irish ollam (“doctor”).

parole.significato: A fool or simpleton; someone out of their senses.
parole.testo: From Irish amadán, introduced into English via literature and political speech.

parole.significato: A clockwork model of any given solar system.
parole.testo: Named after Charles Boyle, 4th Earl of Orrery (1676–1731), for whom such a device was made. The placename is from Irish Orbhraighe, originally the name of a tribe (Orbh-raighe (“Orb's people”)), and then of a territory and a barony.

parole.significato: Fraudulent; fake; having a misleading appearance.
parole.testo: Of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of fawny (“gilt brass ring used by swindlers”) (1781), from Irish fáinne (“ring”).

parole.significato: An evil spell; a curse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish piseog. Doublet of box, pyx, and pyxis.

parole.significato: Magic, witchcraft; a spell, especially one designed to cause or cure illnesses to man or beast, or to increase or decre…
parole.testo: Anglo-Irish, from Irish piseog (“witchcraft”), from Middle Irish piseóc, pisóc.

parole.significato: A kiss.
parole.testo: From Irish póg, from Latin pāx. Doublet of peace.

parole.significato: A freshwater fish, Coregonus pollan, resembling a herring
parole.testo: From Irish pollán.

parole.significato: A kind of small fishing boat from the region of Galway in Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish púcán (“fishing-smack”).

parole.significato: Illegally produced Irish whiskey; moonshine.
parole.testo: From Irish poitín (“little pot; poteen”), from pota (“pot”) (from Middle English potte, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *budn- (“type of vessel”)) + -ín (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A variety of Irish oyster, eaten as a delicacy.
parole.testo: From Pouldoody (name of the inner part of a creek near Corcomroe Abbey in County Clare), possibly from Irish poll Dubhda (literally “O’Dowd’s hole”).

parole.significato: A potato.
parole.testo: From Irish prátaí.

parole.significato: To hit, strike.
parole.testo: From or influenced by Irish poc (“stroke in hurling, bag”). Compare poke (1861).

parole.significato: billy goat
parole.testo: From the Irish poc (“male adult goat, billy goat”). Doublet of buck.

parole.significato: A he-goat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish pocán.

parole.significato: The Irish pound, used as the unit of currency of Ireland until it was replaced by the euro in 2002.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish punt, from Middle English pund. Doublet of funt, pfund, pood, and pound.

parole.significato: nonsense, foolish talk
parole.testo: From Irish ráiméis (“nonsense, poppycock”), from Norman romance. Doublet of romance.

parole.significato: A bandit or brigand.
parole.testo: from Irish rapaire, variant of ropaire (“cutpurse”).

parole.significato: To dye (wool or yarn) reddish-brown by boiling or soaking in water with alder twigs.
parole.testo: From Irish ruaim, from Old Irish rúam (“alder tree; alder bark; dye for wool made from alder bark; dun or red colour”) (probably whence Irish ruaimnigh, Old Irish rúamnaigid (“to dye red”)); further etymology unknown.

parole.significato: An ancient form of unrhymed Old Irish verse that uses alliteration and meter.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Irish rosc (“rhetorical composition”), from Old Irish rosc (“short poem, ode”).

parole.significato: Commotion; rowdiness; uproar; hubbub.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish ruaille buaille.

parole.significato: Synonym of cry uncle.
parole.testo: Unknown. Uncle may be an anglicization of Irish anacal (“protection”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A fraudulent or dishonest deal. A swindle.
parole.testo: US American carnival slang of uncertain origin. Possibly from scamp (“swindler, cheater”) or Irish cam (“crooked”). parole.significato: A whitethorn, hawthorn or similar bush.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish sceach.

parole.significato: An oblong shield of wickerwork once used in Ireland.
parole.testo: From Irish sciath.

parole.significato: A sod of grass-grown turf from the surface of a bog or from a field.
parole.testo: From Irish scrath (“a turf”), sgraith (“a turf, green sod”), akin to Scottish Gaelic sgrath, sgroth (“the outer skin of anything, a turf, a green sod”).

parole.significato: a severe scratch
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish scráib.

parole.significato: To write.
parole.testo: In view of the slang nature of the term, probably from Polari screeve (“write”), from Irish scríobh, eventually from Latin scrībō (“write”). Doublet of shrive.

parole.significato: A yeoman or petty farmer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish scológ.

parole.significato: A tuft or clump of grass.
parole.testo: From Irish.

parole.significato: A bard, genealogist, or storyteller in Gaelic culture.
parole.testo: From Irish seanchaí and Scottish Gaelic seanchaidh, from Old Irish senchaid.

parole.significato: The trefoil leaf of any small clover, especially Trifolium repens, or such a leaf from a clover-like plant, commonly us…
parole.testo: From Irish seamróg, from Old Irish semróc, diminutive of semar, semair (“clover”), from Proto-Celtic *semarā, *semaris (compare Gaulish uisumaris (“clover”)), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *semh₁r-, *smeh₁r-. Related to Old Norse smári (“clover”) and possibly Georgian სამყურა (samq̇ura, “clover”

parole.significato: A wanderer; a vagabond.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish seachrán.

parole.significato: A geared steam locomotive, patented by Ephraim Shay.
parole.testo: Variant of Shea, from Irish Ó Séaghdha.

parole.significato: An unlicensed drinking establishment, especially in Ireland, Scotland, and South Africa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish síbín.

parole.significato: A carving of a naked woman with an exaggerated vulva, found in old British and Irish architecture, perhaps used to ward…
parole.testo: From Irish Síle na gcíoch (“Julia of the breasts”). Attested in English from the 19th century.

parole.significato: To play a deceitful confidence trick on (someone); to swindle, to trick; also, to carry out an act of mischief on (some…
parole.testo: The origin of the noun is uncertain. As the earliest attestations are from California, U.S.A., in the 1850s towards the end of the California gold rush (see the quotations), it is possible that the word derives from one of the following: * Irish sionnachuighim (“to play tricks”, literally “to play t

parole.significato: A ditch, especially a field boundary ditch usually used to drain fields and mark their boundaries.
parole.testo: From Irish seoch, from English sough.

parole.significato: A wooden (traditionally blackthorn (sloe) wood) club ending with a large knob.
parole.testo: From Irish sail éille (“shillelagh”, literally “cudgel of a thong”), altered to match the name of the village of Shillelagh (from Irish Síol Éalaigh (literally “descendants of Éalach”), because the forest near it provided wood from which such clubs could be made.

parole.significato: snail (in its shell)
parole.testo: From Irish seilide (“snail”) búrc.

parole.significato: An Irish person considered excessively Anglophile, an Irish person who acts English or desires to be part of English so…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish Seoinín (“Johnny”), from Seán (“John, John Bull”) + -ín (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A fairy in Gaelic folklore (a member of the Sidhe).
parole.testo: From obsolete Irish sídhe (now spelled sí). See Sidhe for more.

parole.significato: A one-eared spade for cutting turf or peat, consisting of an iron flat-bladed head and a long wooden shaft.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish sleán, sleaghán.

parole.significato: A dishonest person; a trickster, usually from a rural area.
parole.testo: From Irish slíghbhín, slíbhín, with the same meaning; from sliabh (“mountain”) (hence the implication that the person is rural).

parole.significato: An untrustworthy or cunning person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish slíbhín.

parole.significato: A large amount.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish slua (“crowd”) and Scottish Gaelic sluagh (“crowd”), from Middle Irish slúag, from Old Irish slóg, from Proto-Celtic *slougos (“troop, army”), from Proto-Indo-European *slowgʰos, *slowgos (“entourage”).

parole.significato: A hard ball, similar in size to a baseball, used in hurling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish sliotar.

parole.significato: A lazy and slovenly or obese person.
parole.testo: From Irish slaba. Compare slobber, which is of Germanic origin.

parole.significato: A deep cavity formed by the action of subterranean streams common in some limestone districts of Ireland.
parole.testo: From Irish slugaid (“a slough”).

parole.significato: Fragments or splintered pieces; numerous tiny disconnected items.
parole.testo: Uncertain. The following words, all first attested later than the headword, have been compared: * Irish smidiríní, smiodairíní (“smithereens”), from smiodar (“broken piece, fragment”) + -ín (suffix forming diminutive nouns) + -í (slender form of -aí (suffix forming plurals of some nouns)). * smither

parole.significato: Appealing or stylish in appearance or manner; classy, flashy.
parole.testo: Origin unknown; the following etymologies have been suggested: * A blend of sna(ppy) + (ja)zzy. * From Irish snas (“finish, polish; good appearance”) + English -y (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘having the quality of’).

parole.significato: A poor migratory farm worker in Ireland, often viewed as a rascal or mischievous and cunning person.
parole.testo: A late 18th-century term, from Irish spailpín.

parole.significato: Poultry which has been cut along the spine and spread out for more even cooking.
parole.testo: The noun is probably derived from one of the following: * A variant of spitchcock (“eel split lengthwise and broiled”). from Middle English spiche-coke, The further etymology is uncertain; the following possibilities have been suggested: ** From Middle English *speche, *spiche (“to split”) + cock, c

parole.significato: A foot.
parole.testo: From Irish spág (“the paw, limb or claw of an animal”), transferred to humans as pejorative or for club-foot.

parole.significato: A Staffordshire bull terrier.
parole.testo: From Old English stæþ (“landing place”) + ford. As a surname, occasionally derived from Irish (see Stocker).

parole.significato: A layabout or good-for-nothing
parole.testo: From Irish stócach and Scottish Gaelic stòcach (“an idle fellow who lives on the industry of others, a lounger”).

parole.significato: very drunk, intoxicated
parole.testo: Uncertain. The ending -ious appears to be a mock-Latinate jocular formation. parole.significato: A wide, flat river valley.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish srath and Scottish Gaelic srath (“wide, flat river valley, strath; floor of river valley; river meadow”), both from Old Irish srath (“grass, sward; river valley; floor of river valley; river meadow”), from Proto-Celtic *stratos (“valley”), from Proto-Indo-European *str̥h₃tós (“sp

parole.significato: A disreputable woman, a slut.
parole.testo: From Irish straoill (“untidy person”).

parole.significato: A straw rope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish súgán (“rope”), from Proto-Celtic *souggo, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to bend, to cut, to drive”), see also Sanskrit सुवति (suvati). Doublet of soogan.

parole.significato: An Irish Catholic.
parole.testo: From the Irish forename Tadhg (anglicised as Taig or Teague), which was historically one of the commonest names in Ireland. Compare paddy, mick, tim.

parole.significato: The heir presumptive to the chieftainship or kingship of a Celtic clan in ancient Ireland, Scotland or Mann.
parole.testo: From Irish tánaiste (“second-in-command”). Doublet of Tánaiste.

parole.significato: The head of the government of Ireland, comparable to a prime minister of a Commonwealth of Nations country.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish Taoiseach (“chieftain, leader; prime minister of Ireland”). The plural form Taoisigh is borrowed from Irish Taoisigh.

parole.significato: Goodbye.
parole.testo: Possibly from Irish tabhair aire (“take care”).

parole.significato: An Irishman.
parole.testo: From the Irish first name Tadhg. Cognate with English taig (“A Catholic”). Compare Mick and Paddy.

parole.significato: An area of land belonging to a church or monastery
parole.testo: From Irish tearmann, from Middle Irish termonn (“church land affording right of sanctuary”), from Latin terminus (“limit”). Doublet of term and terminus.

parole.significato: An insignificant amount; a trifle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish tráithnín (“a stem of dried grass”).

parole.significato: An extra product given to a customer at no additional charge; a lagniappe.
parole.testo: From Irish tuilleadh (“more”).

parole.significato: Synonym of hillock.
parole.testo: From Irish toman (“small hill, hillock”), diminutive of tom (“hill”).

parole.significato: A member or supporter of the Conservative Party, which evolved from Royalist politicians; historically associated with…
parole.testo: From Irish tóraí (“pursuer”), from tóir (“pursuit”). The first recorded use in English is from a 1646 letter by James Butler, Earl of Ormond, to a Colonel O'Brien, describing bandits and thieves on main roadways.

parole.significato: trousers (or similar garments)
parole.testo: Apparently partly a variant of trews, and perhaps partly from Irish triús.

parole.significato: The fifth group of inhabitants of Ireland according to the Lebor Gabála Érenn tradition, thought to represent the gods…
parole.testo: From Irish Tuatha Dé Danann (literally “peoples of the goddess Danu”).

parole.significato: A temporary lake in an area of limestone, filled by rising groundwater during the rainy winter season.
parole.testo: From Irish tur (“dry”) + loch (“lake”).

parole.significato: To realise something; to catch on; to recognize someone or something.
parole.testo: Possibly from Irish and Scottish Gaelic tuig (“to understand”).

parole.significato: One who plays uilleann pipes.
parole.testo: Partial calque of Irish píobairí uilleann, or from uilleann pipes.

parole.significato: The bagpipes of Ireland, which have a bellows strapped around the wrist and arm to inflate the bag rather than the play…
parole.testo: Partial calque of Irish píb uilleann, literally "elbow pipe".

parole.significato: A lament for the dead.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish [Term?].

parole.significato: whisky
parole.testo: Abbreviation of usquebaugh, from Irish uisce beatha (“water of life”) and Scottish Gaelic uisge beatha (“water of life”). Compare whisky and obsolete whiskybae.

parole.significato: An ostentatiously pious person.
parole.testo: From devotee + -een (from Irish -ín).

parole.significato: Requesting an explanation.
parole.testo: From What's the story with you?, possibly through Irish cad é an scéal (lit. "What's the story") (possible backtranslation).

parole.significato: Exclamation of dismay.
parole.testo: From Irish a Mhuire (“oh Mary”).

parole.significato: An expression of surprise.
parole.testo: From Irish mhuise, originally a euphemism for A Mhuire! (“O Mary!”) in calling upon the Virgin Mary. Compare Irish muise.

parole.significato: In medieval Ireland, a bandit operating in the forest.
parole.testo: From wood + kern. Calque of Irish ceithearn choille.

parole.significato: An exclamation of disbelief, dismissal or asseveration.
parole.testo: From Irish dhera.

parole.significato: Foam rising upon beer or other malt liquors when fermenting, used as leaven in brewing and making bread; yeast.
parole.testo: From Middle English berme, berm, from Old English beorma, from Proto-West Germanic *bermō (“yeast; barm”); related to the dialectal Low German Bärm (“yeast”), from Middle Low German barm, berm. The cake sense is possibly a shortened form of barmcake, which would be made with yeast as described in th

parole.significato: A heavy working shoe; a brogue.
parole.testo: An alteration of brogue. Most dictionaries give the source as Irish *brógán (from bróg (“shoe”) + -án (diminutive suffix)) or its Scottish Gaelic equivalent, but no such word can be confirmed to exist in either language (apart from the given name Brógán, the source of the surname Brogan).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: An assessed tax, duty, or levy; billeting.
parole.testo: For the first meaning below, the writings of Edmund Spenser, published 1633, point to a borrowing from Irish cís (“tax, tribute, cess, rent”), likely from Latin census. Other senses: Uncertain. Occurs in print at least as early as 1831, when Samuel Lover used the expression as one already long-estab

parole.significato: A group of people all descended from a common ancestor, in fact or belief, especially when the exact genealogies are no…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish clann (“offspring, children of the family”) and Scottish Gaelic clann, both from Old Irish cland, borrowed from Old Welsh plant, itself borrowed from Latin planta (“shoot, offspring”). Doublet of plant and planta.

parole.significato: Injured, or not functioning properly (with respect to legs).
parole.testo: Origin obscure and uncertain. Possibly from the English dialectal (North Midlands) adjective game (“lame”), Welsh cam (“crooked”), or from Irish cam (“bent”), by way of Shelta. Compare also Old Occitan gambi (“lame, limping”), related to Old Occitan gamba (“leg”) (see also French jambe (“leg”), Engl

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining, to a Green Party or green party.
parole.testo: English surname, a topographic name for someone who either lived near a village green, or was just fond of the colour. parole.significato: An inexperienced recruit, especially in the police or armed forces.
parole.testo: Thought to be an alteration of recruit + -ie, or from rook (“a cheat”) + -ie. Another possible origin is Dutch broekie (short for broekvent (“a boy still in short trousers”)), a common term for a shipmate. Also suggested is Irish rúca (“an inexperienced person”).
